result.summary: The Chorus sings of Helen's ruinous marriage, the lion cub parable and the curse of arrogance. Agamemnon arrives in triumph with Cassandra, and after a tense exchange Clytaemestra persuades him to walk on purple tapestries into the palace, then prays to Zeus.

scenes.title: Chorus sings of Helen's ruin
scenes.summary: The Chorus reflects on Helen's name, the fall of Troy, the lion cub parable and how iniquity breeds more iniquity.
scenes.stakes: Troy and its people are destroyed by the wrong done to hospitality and to Zeus.

scenes.title: Agamemnon arrives at Argos
scenes.summary: The Chorus welcomes Agamemnon, who greets the gods of Argos, recalls Troy's fall and praises Odysseus as his only loyal helper.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon's safe homecoming and the loyalty of his people are in question.

scenes.title: The purple tapestries
scenes.summary: Clytaemestra declares her devotion and urges Agamemnon to walk on purple tapestries. He reluctantly yields, tells her to receive Cassandra, and enters the palace as she prays to Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon risks the gods' jealousy by treading on tapestries, a presumption that foreshadows his death.

alias_notes.explanation: Agamemnon addresses her by her mother's name.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous pun on Helen's name as ruin (Hell) to ships, men and city.
Agamemnon asks to be honoured as a man, not a god.
Echoes the Greek maxim to call no man happy until his death.

analysis.text: Inherited guilt and hubris run through the ode: wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing, preparing for Agamemnon's fall.
The tapestry scene shows Agamemnon's pride giving way to Clytaemestra's persuasion, with dramatic irony as her words hide murderous intent.

legacy.text: The lion cub parable became a lasting image of a dangerous guest or ally nurtured in one's own house.

fun_facts.text: Purple dye was extremely costly in antiquity, so walking on purple cloth was a display of wasteful, god-like extravagance.

language_notes.text: The Greek name Helene is played on as if from a root meaning 'to destroy' (helein), so Helen's name signals ruin of ships, men and city.
Zephyrus is the west wind; 'earth-born' is an odd epithet, perhaps stressing a wind that blew from the land.
The Greeks follow like hunters tracing the 'vanished track' of oars; the quarry is Helen's ship, beached by the river Simoïs near Troy.
Helen's marriage to Paris is called 'a mourning' (kedos, marriage-bond, punned with 'kêdos', grief). Zeus Xenios, protector of guests, punished Paris's violation of hospitality.
'I trow' means 'I believe'; 'burthen' is an archaic form of 'burden'.
'Ruth' means sorrow or pity; 'warder of host and guest' refers to Zeus as protector of hospitality.
'Arrogance' translates hybris, overweening pride that defies the gods; 'Recklessness' is its offspring.
"Offspring of Atreus" means son of Atreus; Agamemnon is addressed by his lineage, a formal mode of greeting.
"Ramament" is a rare word for an armament, the assembled army and fleet sent against Troy.
Refers to the sacrifice of Iphigenia and the war's heavy losses; the Chorus admits it once disapproved of the expedition.
Imagery of a voting court: the gods cast ballots into an urn for Troy's destruction, while the urn of acquittal stayed empty.
The "brood of the horse" is the Greek army that emerged from the wooden horse; the Pleiads setting marks the season, around late autumn.
Odysseus reportedly feigned madness to avoid joining the expedition, hence "sailed against his will."
"Cautery or the knife" means burning or cutting out disease, here used for harsh remedies against disloyalty in the state.
Burghers are citizens of a town; here the Elders of Argos, the chorus, are addressed as representatives of the city.
Geryon was a mythical monster with three bodies, killed by Heracles. Clytaemestra says Agamemnon would have needed his three bodies to die as often as rumour claimed.
The 'high-hung halter' means a noose; she says she was nearly driven to hang herself by despair, and others cut her down.
'Forestay' is a rope bracing the ship's mast; 'saviour forestay' means the support that keeps the vessel safe.
'Car' means chariot; 'liege' is a respectful address to a lord.
Agamemnon says her speech is as long as his absence, a dry jibe at her length.
'Barbarian' means non-Greek, especially Eastern; Greeks associated prostration before rulers with Persian custom, which Agamemnon rejects.
"Broideries" means embroideries: here the richly dyed, embroidered tapestries laid out for Agamemnon to walk on.
"Cavillings" are petty, carping criticisms or objections.
A paradox: one who is not envied has nothing enviable about him, so envy is the price of success.
"Slave-like" because sandals are servile footwear; Agamemnon asks a servant to remove them before he treads the cloth, a gesture of humility.
Greeks believed the gods resented excessive human pride and prosperity; walking on costly cloth reserved for gods might provoke their jealous "eye".
"Yon stranger damsel" is Cassandra, the captive Trojan princess he brings home; he asks Clytaemestra to treat her kindly.
Refers to a vow made at an oracle's shrine, promising to sacrifice precious things for Agamemnon's safe return.
"Dog-star" is Sirius, whose rising marks the hottest summer days.

context_notes.text: Helen, wife of Menelaus, left Sparta with Paris, a prince of Troy, which caused the Trojan War.
Ilium is another name for Troy; Paris was Priam's son, and the Trojans had celebrated the wedding song.
The 'old saying' held that great prosperity inevitably brings misfortune; the Chorus will reject it in the next lines.
Argos is Agamemnon's kingdom; he thanks its local gods first, as a returning king would, before entering his palace.
The purple tapestries prepare Clytaemestra's famous scene, in which she lures Agamemnon to walk on costly cloth, an act of hubris.
Strophius of Phocis was a friend of the family; Orestes, sent to him for safety, will later return to avenge his father.
Walking on purple dyed cloth was costly and reserved for gods; the act will be seen as arrogant (hubris).
Leda was Clytaemestra's mother, by Tyndareus; Helen was her sister.
Priam was king of Troy, whom Agamemnon defeated. Clytaemestra suggests even a proud Eastern king would have accepted such honour.
Cassandra, daughter of Priam, was given to Agamemnon as war-prize. Apollo had cursed her prophecies never to be believed.
Purple dye came from sea-shellfish and was extremely costly, so trampling it was a conspicuous waste, and a ritual offence.

literary_notes.text: The lion cub story is an extended allegory: the charming guest who grows into a destroyer stands for Helen and the ruin she brings Troy.
The cub's gentle early life sets up the coming violence, hinting that Helen's charm conceals disaster.
The lion becomes a 'priest of ruin', a sacrificial figure whose feast is slaughter, suggesting divine will behind the destruction.
Righteousness is a goddess who shines in humble homes and turns away from corrupt wealth, voicing the Chorus's moral view.
The king as a discerning shepherd of his flock presents rule as guardianship and warns that flatterers' eyes can deceive.
The Greek army becomes a ravening lion drinking princely blood, conveying savage violence in victory.
"Mirror of companionship" and "shadow of a shade" depict false friends as empty reflections with no substance.
Agamemnon credits the gods with bringing him home safely, while the audience knows death awaits him inside his palace.
The image of a net riddled with holes exaggerates the wounds rumour reported, showing her anxiety through vivid overstatement.
The string of images (watch-dog, pillar, land seen at sea) piles up flattery, which seems excessive and hints at insincerity.
Justice ushering him home is darkly ironic: Clytaemestra means his death, and Justice will indeed greet him as avenger of Iphigenia.
Agamemnon's remark that no man is happy until his life ends well foreshadows his own imminent death.
Agamemnon's quick reply gives away his own pride; he admits that even Priam would have done what he is hesitant to do.
Rapid one-line exchanges let Clytaemestra's persuasion outmatch Agamemnon's resistance step by step.
Agamemnon is a root that revives the house's leaves and shade, and a summer coolness; the images of nature hide menace.
Her prayer to Zeus the Fulfiller sounds pious, but the audience knows she means to fulfil his murder.
